articles.title: Scientists planted 133 portable seismometers around Yellowstoneâs Old Faithful for two weeks; tiny ground vibrations revealed an underground hot-water reservoir holding about 79 million gallons
articles.summary: US News: Old Faithful may be the worldâs most famous geyser, but until recently, no one had a clear picture of the âplumbingâ that powers its eruptions. In a l.
articles.body: Old Faithful may be the worldâs most famous geyser, but until recently, no one had a clear picture of the âplumbingâ that powers its eruptions. In a landmark 2017 studytitled 'Anatomy of Old Faithful From Subsurface Seismic Imaging of the Yellowstone Upper Geyser Basin', University of Utah scientists deployed 133 small, portable seismometers around Old Faithful and nearby Geyser Hill for two weeks, listening to the faint hum of the ground between eruptions. By turning everyday micro-vibrations, caused by wind, water, tourists, and the geyserâs own boiling, into a usable signal, the team mapped a hidden reservouir of hot water beneath the surface. Their analysis suggests the reservoir can hold roughly 300,000 cubic meters of water, or about 79 million gallons. Based on the reportings from the University of Utah and the U.S. Geological Surveyâs Yellowstone Volcano Observatory, here's more details about the discovery:Why Old Faithfulâs underground system was a mysteryOld Faithful erupts like clockwork every 44 to 125 minutes, drawing millions of visitors to Yellowstone National Park each year. Yet despite its fame, the near-surface geology and fluid pathways feeding the geyser were poorly understood. Deep magma reservoirs 5â40 km below the park provide heat, but the shallow âplumbingâ that channels hot water to the vent had never been mapped in detail. Traditional seismic methods that rely on large earthquakes or active sources (like hammer strikes or small explosions) arenât ideal in a sensitive, crowded tourist area. The National Park Service specifically asked researchers to survey the Old Faithful area to better manage buildings and walkways constructed over thermal features that can create excessive subsurface heat.Turning noise into a map: the 133-seismometer experimentTo capture the subtle signals, the University of Utah team used compact, autonomous seismometers developed for the oil and gas industry. Each unit is a white canister about six inches high, self-contained and inexpensive compared to traditional instruments that can cost over $10,000. In 2015, researchers placed 133 of these sensors around Old Faithful and Geyser Hill for a two-week campaign, creating a dense network capable of detecting tiny ground movements.Instead of creating their own seismic source, the scientists treated ambient noise as data. They used continuous ground shaking from humans, cars, wind, water, and Yellowstoneâs hydrothermal activity, then extracted coherent signals from the background vibration. Doctoral student Sin-Mei Wu and co-author Fan-Chi Lin developed analysis methods that correlated signals from sensors near persistent hydrothermal sources to others across the array, effectively using the geyser system itself as a seismic source. This approach allowed them to image shallow structures without disturbing the fragile environment of the Upper Geyser Basin.What the tremors revealed: a giant hidden reservoirThe sensors recorded a striking pattern: bursts of intense seismic tremors around Old Faithful lasting about 60 minutes, separated by roughly 30 minutes of quiet. Counterintuitively, the eruption does not occur at the peak of shaking but at the end, just before the tremors subside. After an eruption, the geyserâs underground cavity refills with hot water. As it fills, pressurized bubbles rise, cool rapidly, and implode; the energy from these implosions generates the pre-eruption tremors.When analyzing the data, the team noticed that tremor signals from Old Faithful were not reaching the western boardwalk. Seismic waves from another hydrothermal feature to the north also slowed and scattered in nearly the same area. With the dense sensor network, they could pinpoint the shape, size, and location of the anomaly: Old Faithfulâs hydrothermal reservoir. Wu estimates the reservoirâa network of cracks and fractures through which water flows, is about 200 meters in diameter, slightly larger than the University of Utahâs Rice-Eccles Stadium, and can hold approximately 300,000 cubic meters of water, or more than 79 million gallons. By comparison, each eruption releases only around 30 cubic meters (nearly 8,000 gallons), meaning the reservoir is vastly larger than any single eruption.Why this matters for science and park managementMapping Old Faithfulâs underground system does more than satisfy curiosity. It helps park managers understand where heat and fluid flow beneath buildings, walkways, and visitor areas, informing safer infrastructure planning in one of the worldâs most visited geothermal zones. The study also demonstrates a powerful, low-impact method for imaging shallow geology in sensitive environments by leveraging ambient noise instead of active sources.For researchers, the work opens new questions about how subsurface structures change over time and how seismic waves propagate through hydrothermal systems. The team returned for additional surveys in 2016 and planned further deployments, aiming to produce even higher-resolution images and explore other basins like Norris, the parkâs hottest geothermal area. As Fan-Chi Lin noted, breakthroughs in Yellowstone depend on both new techniques and long-term relationships with the park: a reminder that some of the most iconic natural wonders still have secrets waiting beneath the surface.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 1,000 people in Japan join forces to pull a 400-ton castle keep back toward its original position after it was moved 78 meters for repairs
articles.summary: Rest of World News: About 1,000 people in Japan joined forces on Sunday to help pull the roughly 400-ton keep of Hirosaki Castle back toward its original position, more t.
articles.body: About 1,000 people in Japan joined forces on Sunday to help pull the roughly 400-ton keep of Hirosaki Castle back toward its original position, more than a decade after the historic structure was moved nearly 78 meters for repairs. Participants in Aomori Prefecture were divided into groups and used ropes to pull a cart carrying the castle keep, moving the massive structure 109 centimeters closer to its original location. The unusual public event is part of a major restoration project aimed at returning the keep to where it stood before its relocation in 2015. About 4,000 people are scheduled to participate in similar events, with the public effort expected to move the keep about 5 meters in total as the centuries-old castle begins its journey home.1,000 people pull 400-ton castle keep toward its original positionThe rope-pulling event took place at Hirosaki Castle in Aomori Prefecture, northeastern Japan, on August 23, with about 1,000 people selected by lottery taking part. Participants were divided into groups and pulled ropes attached to a cart carrying the roughly 400-ton keep. Their combined effort moved the structure 109 centimeters toward its original position. The event is part of a series of public participation activities scheduled between August 22 and 30, with about 4,000 people expected to take part. Together, the events are intended to move the keep about 5 meters, allowing members of the public to play a direct role in the highly unusual restoration project. One participant, 16-year-old high school student Mei Umetsu, said she had also helped pull the keep 11 years earlier when it was moved away from its original site.Why the castle keep was moved 78 meters in 2015The keep was moved in 2015 because the stone walls supporting Hirosaki Castle needed extensive repairs. Rather than dismantling the historic structure itself, restoration teams moved the keep away from its original foundation so workers could safely work on the aging masonry underneath it. The keep was shifted approximately 77.6 meters, or about 78 meters, from its original position. The relocation allowed specialists to dismantle and rebuild the supporting stone wall while protecting the historic wooden keep. The current project is effectively reversing that earlier move, with the keep now being returned to the location it occupied before the repairs began.How Japan repaired the castleâs historic stone wallsThe restoration of Hirosaki Castleâs stone walls was a major undertaking involving thousands of individual stones. According to Hirosaki City, workers dismantled and documented 2,185 stones before rebuilding the wall. The stones were carefully recorded so they could be returned to their appropriate positions during reconstruction, helping preserve the historic character and construction methods of the castle. The stone-wall rebuilding was completed in December 2024, clearing an important stage of the restoration project and allowing preparations for the keepâs return to move forward. Further structural and seismic work is also planned to improve the stability of the castle and protect it for the future.The 400-ton keep is slowly making its way homeThe August rope-pulling event represents only a small part of the keepâs approximately 78-meter journey back to its original position. The public events are designed to move the structure around 5 meters in total, while the remaining distance will be covered through the broader restoration operation. Officials plan to have the keep returned to its original location by the end of 2026. The spectacle of people physically pulling such a massive historic structure has attracted attention because it combines traditional methods, modern engineering and community participation. The operation is carefully planned to ensure that the centuries-old keep can be moved without damaging the historic structure.What happens to Hirosaki Castle after the moveThe return of the keep will not mark the end of the restoration project. Additional preservation and seismic reinforcement work will continue after the structure reaches its original position. The keep is one of Japanâs 12 surviving original castle keeps and is the only surviving original keep in the Tohoku region, making its preservation particularly significant. The present three-story keep dates to 1810, after an earlier castle tower was destroyed by fire. Hirosaki Castle itself was originally constructed in 1611. The keepâs interior has been closed to visitors since November 2025 and is expected to remain closed for several years while further preservation work is carried out, meaning the remarkable return journey is only one stage in the long-term effort to protect the historic castle.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: China hits out at 'illegal' new US sanctions on Iran and trading partners
articles.summary: The US has threatened to isolate nations that continue to do business with Tehran, which sells much of its oil to Beijing.
articles.body:
China has vowed to protect its interests after the US announced plans to widen economic sanctions against Iran and its trading partners, which include Beijing.

Foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said China was firmly opposed to what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights.

This came after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the new measures on Monday, warning any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.

China is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, although the trade has declined under the US blockade of Iran's ports.

Lin said: "Cooperation between China and Iran has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be interfered with or disrupted."

Bessent described the plans for sanctions as "the single greatest financial offensive ever" against Iran, warning banks and businesses would share in Iran's isolation if they refused to cut ties with the country.

He declined to focus on specific nations, but said US President Donald Trump would be phoning world leaders "with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime".

However, responding to a question about Chinese banks, Bessent said he wanted to make clear "no one was above the reach of US sanctions".

The announcement comes ahead of planned talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month.

Washington is likely to be wary of potential retaliation from Beijing, which processes the majority of the world's rare earths and other critical minerals, crucial in the manufacture of many high-tech products.

Beijing has already tightened export controls on rare earths as part of previous trade negotiations with the US.

China's response followed Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh saying Tehran was "fully prepared" for the wider sanctions, which he said would lead to "another defeat" for the US.

"The government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," he told state television.

"We also have our own tools and know how to play the game," he said, adding Tehran had been "waiting for these plans for a long time".

Iran says it is 'fully prepared' to counter widened US economic sanctions Published 16 hours ago

Iran says it is 'fully prepared' to counter widened US economic sanctions

The US has dubbed its latest sanctions "Operation Economic Outcast" and described them as an "economic D-Day" against Iran.

It comes almost six months after the start of the Iran war.

The conflict has since led to hikes in oil prices worldwide, with Tehran effectively blocking exports through the Strait of Hormuz - a waterway vital to the global economy. The US has also slowed traffic via its own naval blockade.

Recent attempts to end the conflict via diplomacy have failed, and a 60-day ceasefire formally expired last week with no sign of a settlement.

With the announcement of new sanctions, the US treasury secretary claimed America was "no longer managing the Iranian threat, we are ending it".

UK Chancellor John Healey said the British government supported "US work to secure a diplomatic solution and welcome efforts to increase pressure".

Iran is already under heavy sanctions from the US, but Bessent said these go further.

He said the Treasury had mapped financial channels, facilitators and networks used by Iran to evade sanctions to trade oil, imposing sanctions on almost 60 entities, individuals and vessels.

But analysts had cast doubt on the latest measures even before China's response.

David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, told the BBC the direct impact on Iran's energy revenues would be "somewhat of a damp squib".

"We suspect that the new package will have only a limited direct impact on Iranian energy flows in the short term," he added.

This is partly due to the fact roughly 90% of Iran's oil goes to China, he said, "which has not recognised US sanctions in the past and is unlikely to be cowed this time either".

Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa Program at the International Crisis Group, said: "Generally, the Chinese are against unilateral sanctions. They would comply with multilateral or international sanctions, but unilateral sanctions just imposed by the US - they have always seen that as illegitimate."

And although Iran's neighbours like Pakistan, Turkey and Iraq want to maintain good relationships with the US, they "can't really afford to cut off ties with Iran", Vaez told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

He said putting economic pressure on Tehran "doesn't work" because the Iranian regime is willing to "absorb any pain" and pass it onto the people.

Other trade partners that could be affected by the US announcement include India and Russia, who have not yet responded.

articles.title: DUP MP Gregory Campbell to face expenses probe
articles.summary: The watchdog's investigation concerns the MPâs spendingÂ against theirÂ OfficeÂ CostsÂ budget.Â Â
articles.body:
The parliamentary watchdog has launched an investigation into the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) MP Gregory Campbell over potential spending breaches.

The Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority (IPSA) said it will determine whether Campbell has been "paid an amount under the Scheme of MPs Staffing and Business Costs , external that should not have been allowed".

No further information will be published until the investigation has concluded.

A DUP spokesperson said: "Gregory Campbell has spent twenty-five years working for the people of East Londonderry.

"He is one of the most active constituency MPs and consistently has one of the lowest costs of NI MPs."

The party claim this is a "politicised complaint" made against Campbell about information cards and leaflets he personally distributes throughout his constituency weekly.

"Mr Campbell had already provided information about this matter and will fully cooperate with the investigation."

They added that while the process is ongoing, he "will make no further comment".

articles.title: Highland Council tourist tax of £5 a night could raise £9.5m a year
articles.summary: Councillors have agreed to hold a consultation on proposals to introduce the visitor levy.
articles.body:
Highland Council is to hold a public consultation on its plans for a £5 per room, per night visitor levy for stays in hotels, B&Bs and short-term lets.

The proposed charge for hostels and campsites would be £2 per night.

A meeting of the full council in Inverness heard that the local authority had been discussing a proposed tourist tax for seven years.

Councillors were told that if the fixed-rate visitor levy went ahead it could raise about £9.5m a year to help pay for infrastructure such as roads.

Under the plans, the charges would apply across the whole Highland Council area for nine months of the year, excluding December, January and February.

Accommodation providers would retain 5% of the levy collected to help cover administration costs.

Research suggests the Highlands has almost 9.4 million annual visitors.

Council leader and SNP councillor, Raymond Bremner, said the local authority had been "labouring" at trying to introduce a charge for "a long time".

He said "most people" in the Highlands supported the idea of a levy, and he put forward a motion backing a public consultation.

Scottish Green Party councillor Chris Ballance said the charges could generate much-needed money for social housing, but he had concerns the levy would hit lower income families visiting the Highlands more than those able to afford luxury accommodation.

Liberal Democrat councillors tabled an amendment requesting that it be made clear that Highland residents would not pay the fees if visiting another part of the region.

They said residents should not be expected to pay an additional "tax", and it would also avoid a situation where people travelling for hospital appointments in Inverness having to claim expenses from NHS Highland.

More stories from the Highlands and Islands

News from the Highlands and Islands on BBC Sounds

Scottish Conservative councillors put forward an amendment calling for a decision on the consultation to be delayed until the results of an independent economic impact assessment were known in the coming weeks.

They said the assessment could show a negative impact on tourist visits and a potential legal challenge from tourism businesses.

Both amendments failed to get enough support and the motion was voted through.

Raymond Bremner said the council would encourage as wide a consultation as possible.

The Association of Scotland's Self-Caterers said the proposed tiered fixed rate was simpler than Highland Council's original plan for a percentage-based levy.

But the association's chief executive Fiona Campbell said councillors should have waited for the results of an independent economic impact assessment before agreeing to consult.

"Businesses and communities deserve to see the full picture of what this levy could mean before they're asked to make an informed judgement," she said.

Before the meeting, the Highland Hotel Association (HHA) said £5 was too high and suggested a lower rate of £3.

HHA said its data suggested summer occupancy rates across the region have dropped by 10% compared to last year, while costs for the sector continue to rise.

HHA chairman Craig Ewan said: "Our message to Highland Council is clear: it is not 'no' to a visitor levy, but 'not now'.

"The industry is battling a perfect storm of soaring operating costs and weakening demand."

Edinburgh was the first city in Scotland to introduce a tourist tax earlier this summer.

People staying overnight in hotels, bed and breakfasts and self-catering accommodation are charged an additional 5% on top of their original booking.

It is expected to raise about £50m annually, which could be used to fund new housing, cultural initiatives and a wider police presence.

A similar 5% levy is due to come into force in Glasgow from January 2027, while in Aberdeen a 7% charge will be introduced in April 2027 at the earliest.

The Scottish Borders, Dumfries and Galloway, Orkney and Shetland have rejected proposals for a visitor levy.

articles.title: Row breaks out over minister Anna Turley's A66 crash tribute
articles.summary: Home Office Minister Anna Turley paid tribute to all seven victims initially, sparking a backlash from the shadow justice secretary.
articles.body:
A row has broken out after a Home Office minister paid tribute to all seven victims of the deadly A66 crash.

Anna Turley, who is also MP for the area where the crash took place, was accused by shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy of placing five men who were in a car travelling on the wrong side of the road "on a par" with two police officers in an oncoming car they collided with.

All seven died in the crash near Middlesbrough in the early hours of Saturday, which detectives said resulted from "serious criminal activity".

Turley said Cleveland Police "had specifically requested" she pay tribute to all victims in any message. The force declined to confirm or deny this when contacted by the BBC.

In a letter, Turley accused Timothy of having "sought to create media hits and political points" which was "beneath contempt".

She said there was no "moral equivalence, or judgements about worth" in her tribute.

The row centres on a lengthy Facebook post Turley made shortly after the incident, in which she wrote: "This morning I went down to South Bank to lay flowers and pay my respects, on behalf of our whole community, to the seven people whose lives were so tragically cut short yesterday."

Timothy took issue with that in an X post on Monday night, saying he did not wish to "speak ill of the dead" but that "we should be able to see the difference between right and wrong".

He said it did not feel right for a Home Office minister to equate the two police officers with the men in the other car.

In her reply, Turley said she was "utterly appalled" by the accusation and said she did not know the identities of who had died at the time of her tribute, other than PCs Matthew Blades, 37, and Tom Clough, 38, who she named.

While she said Cleveland Police had asked her to pay tribute to all victims, the force has not confirmed this and the area's police and crime commissioner told the BBC it does not issue media advice regarding police incidents.

Police later confirmed that Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and 17-year-old Cole Robert Worthy were all in the car on the wrong side of the A66. All bar Cahill had previous convictions.

The Volkswagen Passat was being pursued by police until 10 seconds before the crash , according to the police watchdog.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said the Passat was believed to be using cloned registration plates.

Cleveland Police announced five more arrests on Tuesday, bringing the total to 17, including a 16-year-old boy and two men, 18 and 21, arrested on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group.

Separately, two men previously arrested have since been charged as part of the investigation.

articles.title: Mass cancellation of nonimmigrant US visa appointments triggers panic: State Department says it's for training
articles.summary: US News: Thousands of visa applicants all across the world received emails from their embassies and consulates that their visa appointment has been cancelled a.
articles.body: Thousands of visa applicants all across the world received emails from their embassies and consulates that their visa appointment has been cancelled and will be rescheduled only after September 1. This happened to non-immigrant visa applicants, which include student visas, work visas, tourism visas, etc. The emails spread panic as they came in the backdrop of several visa-related developments coming from the State Department. These mass cancellations were reported not from any specific country but sporadically from all across."We regret to inform you that your upcoming nonimmigrant visa interview appointment has been cancelled. Your interview cannot be accommodated until after 1 September 2026. You may apply at the US Embassy/Consulate in your country of nationality. We regret any inconvenience this may cause," one Redditor reported receiving this mail from non-immigrant visa unit of US embassy, Saudi Arabia.State Department's order to all embassies and consulatesThe New York Times reported that this was an instruction from the State Department to all embassies and consulates that they must reschedule all visa interviews until consular offices complete training sessions on a "more restrictive policy". And these training sessions will take place this week. And hence, the State Department sent this instruction to all offices on Monday, triggering the cancellations.In these training sessions, consular officers will be trained to deny immigrant visas (Green Card application, asylum) to applicants who will depend on government aid if they are in the United States.âIn early August, we launched a global training initiative at all of our embassies and consulates worldwide. To accommodate this in-depth training, appointments for visa services will be adjusted," the State Department said to New York Times.The cancellation emails sent shockwaves to applicants, as a similar rescheduling of appointments announced in December 2025 led to major chaos and a bottleneck, and there is still a backlog because of that rescheduling, which was necessitated by the new rule of social media vetting for H-1B visa holders.The NYT report said that separate of this emergency appointment cancellation order, the Trump administration is planning to revoke visas of foreign citizens who came to the US for tourism or business but then applied for asylum to become a permanent resident. The department has started reviewing such visas and around 200,000 people are estimated to become illegal if the government cracks down on these visas.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Georgia sheriffâs office arrested a second deputy in one month over alleged Flock misuse; latest case involved someone he had a personal relationship with
articles.summary: US News: A second Habersham County Sheriff's Office deputy has been fired and arrested in less than a month after an internal audit found he allegedly used the.
articles.body: A second Habersham County Sheriff's Office deputy has been fired and arrested in less than a month after an internal audit found he allegedly used the department's automated license plate reader system to track someone with whom he had a personal relationship. Former deputy Jonathan Thomas, who joined the department on 2 December 2024, was arrested during an ongoing review of how officers use surveillance technology. Thomas has been charged with felony violation of oath of office and a misdemeanor count of misusing license plate data, according to a statement from the Habersham County Sheriff's Office reported by 11Alive. He was later booked into the Habersham County Detention Center. Thomas's dismissal is the second case in several weeks involving alleged misuse of the agency's Flock Safety system. It follows the late July arrest of former deputy Christian Brewer, who faced the same charges after allegedly using the database to track someone he knew personally.Internal review finds second caseThe latest case was uncovered during a wider review by department leaders to make sure access to the database was being used only for legitimate law enforcement investigations. "As we continue to conduct our audit into the use of our Flock system, we have discovered a second deputy who accessed Flock outside of its intended law enforcement purpose," said Habersham County Sheriff Robin Krockum in a public statement reported by 11Alive. The July arrest of Brewer, who had worked for the sheriff's office since May 2024, led command staff to expand their checks of the system. In that case, WSB-TV Channel 2 reported that Krockum personally addressed the misuse and stressed the importance of public trust. "The people of Habersham County trust us with authority and access to sensitive information," Krockum said in a statement published by WSB-TV. "This trust is earned every day and can be lost in a single decision. Any misuse of our authority or the tools provided to your deputies is a betrayal of that trust. Although this was an isolated incident, I will not tolerate misconduct. We will hold our own accountable because the public we serve deserves no less."New rules for surveillance accessFollowing the two cases, the Habersham County Sheriff's Office has introduced tighter rules for accessing license plate data. According to WSB-TV Channel 2 and All On Georgia, the agency reduced the number of employees allowed to conduct certain license plate searches from 39 to 23 designated supervisory officers. Under the new rules, deputies can no longer search the regional database on their own. Every search must first be approved by a supervisor. The supervisor must record the reason for the search and enter a valid, active criminal case number into the system. Deputies must also contact the county dispatch centre by radio so that every search is recorded in the official log. "We will continue to audit our system and hold those accountable who have abused this system," Krockum said in a statement published by 11Alive. "We will continue to be transparent to the public in the way we conduct ourselves and hold those responsible who violate their trust." Flock Safety technology uses networks of fixed cameras to photograph passing vehicles. The cameras record licence plates, vehicle make, model, colour and other identifying features, along with the time and location of each image. The system does not directly show vehicle ownership or personal driver records. However, it stores location data for 30 days, allowing authorised users to see where a particular vehicle has travelled across participating areas.Georgia faces wider scrutinyThe two Habersham County arrests are part of a wider focus on the use of automated camera systems by law enforcement agencies across Georgia. Reports from Hoodline and Now Georgia say internal audits and investigations by the Georgia Bureau of Investigation have led to criminal charges or resignations involving more than 20 law enforcement employees across the state over unauthorised searches of surveillance data. Recent cases include four former Savannah Police Department employees who were arrested following an internal review. Three former Bibb County Sheriff's Office deputies were also charged with stalking and unlawfully keeping license plate information after allegedly accessing records involving personal acquaintances. Similar investigations into camera and license plate data have taken place in Cherokee, DeKalb, Coweta, Greene and Albany counties. The felony charges against the former Habersham County deputies fall under Georgia Code Â§ 16-10-1, which covers violation of oath by a public officer. A conviction can carry a prison sentence of one to five years. The related misdemeanor charge falls under Georgia Code Â§ 35-1-22, which sets rules for the use of automated license plate reader data and prohibits searches that are not for official purposes. The Habersham County Sheriff's Office said the criminal investigation into Thomas remains active. Once the investigation is complete, the final case file will be sent to the District Attorney's Office for further legal proceedings.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Kishor challenges Bihar CM Samrat Choudhary, leader of oppn Tejashwi to clear Class 10 exam
articles.summary: PATNA: Jan Suraaj Party founder Prashant Kishor on Tuesday challenged Bihar chief minister Samrat Choudhary and leader of the opposition Tejashwi Yada.
articles.body: PATNA: Jan Suraaj Party founder Prashant Kishor on Tuesday challenged Bihar chief minister Samrat Choudhary and leader of the opposition Tejashwi Yadav to "sit for their matriculation exams together" and clear the test, news agency PTI reported.Kishor suggested that education minister Mithilesh Tiwari should propose such a move at the next cabinet meeting.As per the PTI report, the Bankipur MLA made the tongue-in-cheek remark while responding to questions from journalists about Tiwari advising Yadav "to clear his Class 10 exams before supporting protests by students".The 49-year-old said, "Tiwari should give the same suggestion to Samrat Choudhary as well. Let him propose in the next cabinet meeting that both the CM and the LoP sit for their matriculation exams together".Yadav is the RJD working president and a decade Kishor's junior, while Choudhary is in his late 50s.The RJD leader had given up studies after flunking in Class 9.Kishor had earlier claimed that Choudhary, who now stated to possess a DLitt degree, had said in his affidavit for the 2010 election that he was Class 7 pass.The former poll strategist said, "I, too, appeal to the two leaders to take up the challenge, on behalf of the state's youth".People of Bihar should have the confidence that their leaders are capable of clearing their class 10 exams, Kishor said, adding: "Choudhary and Yadav must rise to the challenge."(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Patna | Silver Rate in Patna | Bank Holidays in Patna | Public Holidays in Patna | Patna AQI | Weather in Patna | Petrol Price in Patna | Diesel Price in Patna | CNG Price in Patna | LPG Price in PatnaStay updated with the latest Patna news. articles.title: Mamdani faces lawsuit from business group over plan to open five city-owned grocery stores in NYC
articles.summary: US News: A New York City business group representing hundreds of small supermarkets and bodegas has sued Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the city, challenging his pla.
articles.body: A New York City business group representing hundreds of small supermarkets and bodegas has sued Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the city, challenging his plan to open five municipally owned grocery stores.The Multicultural Business Coalition filed two lawsuits in New York County Supreme Court on Monday, arguing that the initiative would hurt small, immigrant- and minority-owned grocery businesses that cannot compete with the discounts offered by city-run stores.The group claims the stores could drive smaller grocers out of business because they would benefit from government subsidies and lower operating costs.âYou cannot expect hard-working small business owners to compete with a supermarket that isnât going to pay rent,â the groupâs general counsel Mark Jaffe told CNN.He argued that independent stores would have no way to match the cityâs prices without similar subsidies.Mamdani, however, defended the initiative, saying he remained confident about both its legality and importance.âWe are talking about delivering five city-run grocery stores in a city of 8.5 million people that has more than a thousand grocery stores,â Mamdani said at a news conference on Monday.The mayor has made the grocery store plan a key part of his affordability agenda. The stores are expected to sell produce, meat, seafood, dairy products and other staples at prices about 30 per cent below typical retail rates.The administration estimates the programme could reduce New Yorkersâ average grocery bills by about 15 per cent, or roughly USD 90 a month.The first city-run grocery store is planned for Hunts Point in the Bronx and is expected to open in 2027. Four more stores are planned across the city, with one in each borough.The lawsuits also allege that city officials failed to properly assess the potential impact of the stores on existing neighbourhood grocers before selecting locations.A second lawsuit argues that the city does not have the legal authority to establish the municipally owned grocery stores.Mamdani pointed to existing subsidised food markets in Manhattan and Brooklyn, arguing that they have not harmed nearby bodegas or grocery stores.The city's Economic Development Corporation, which is overseeing the programme, has said it is also examining tax breaks, incentives and zoning benefits to help ease cost pressures on local grocers.The city has set aside about USD 70 million for the grocery store initiative and is seeking outside operators to run the stores.The legal challenge is the latest in a series of court battles involving major affordability measures proposed by Mamdani's administration.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces group says it has dissolved after merging with the Syrian army
articles.summary: The commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces on Tuesday announced the official dissolution of the group, which once controlled a de facto autono...
articles.body:
DAMASCUS, Syria (AP) — The commander of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces on Tuesday announced the official dissolution of the group, which once controlled a de facto autonomous zone in Syria's northeast.

Speaking during a news conference at the presidential palace in Damascus, Mazloum Abdi said the SDF has completed a merger with the Syrian army and would cease to operate as an independent force. The Kurdish-led force lost most of its territory in northeast Syria to a government offensive in January and then signed the deal to merge with the army.

The SDF was once the main partner of the United States in Syria as it battled the Islamic State group. But after the ouster of former Syrian President Bashar Assad in December 2024, Washington formed close ties with the new government in Damascus led by interim Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa, the former leader of an Islamist insurgent group.

The SDF "carried a heavy responsibility during one of the most difficult periods in Syria's history," Abdi said.

"Today, circumstances have changed, and the country has entered a new phase, one of peace and participation in building a new Syria," he said, announcing the "end of the SDF's mission" and "its dissolution as an independent military force."

Under the 50-year rule of the Assad dynasty in Syria, Kurds were marginalized, with many denied citizenship. Public celebrations of the Nowruz holiday — an ancient Persian springtime new year festival that is also celebrated by Kurds in Syria, Turkey and Iraq as well as Iran — were banned.

Shortly after the uprising against the Assad government began in 2011, the Kurds filled the vacuum created by the withdrawal of government forces from wide areas of Syria's northeast. The SDF at one point controlled about 25% of Syria.

The Kurds were initially circumspect about the new post-Assad government and unwilling to give up their de facto autonomy. Some of the insurgent groups that took part in the offensive that ousted Assad were Turkish-backed forces that had clashed with the SDF in the past.

Turkey considered the SDF to be a terrorist organization because of its ties to the Kurdistan Workers' Party, or PKK, a separatist group that staged a decades-long insurgency in Turkey. A peace process is now underway.

Kurds questioned whether the new Sunni Arab-led authorities would give them true representation in the new government, while al-Sharaa tried to woo them.

During ceasefire negotiations with the SDF in January, he issued a decree strengthening Kurdish rights. It made Kurdish an official language along with Arabic, and adopted Nowruz as a national holiday. It also restored the citizenship of tens of thousands of Kurds in northeastern Hassakeh province after they were stripped of it during the 1962 census.

Abdi said that al-Sharaa had promised that Kurds would have the right to education in their own language, an important issue for the country's Kurdish population.

Questions remain, including the fate of the SDF's all-female fighting units — a sensitive point in the integration talks as many of the Damascus leaders come from a conservative background and are opposed to women in combat.

But the success of the integration agreement with the SDF is a major boost to al-Sharaa's government, which has struggled to unify the country as it begins to recover from a nearly 14-year civil war. Most of the country is now under the control of the central government in Damascus.

The exception is southern Syria's Sweida province, which is now controlled by Druze factions that are hostile to Damascus after clashes last year in which government-affiliated fighters launched sectarian revenge attacks on Druze civilians. The Druze factions have received support from Israel, which is also occupying a strip of land in southern Syria near the border with the Israeli-annexed Golan Heights.

articles.title: New Mexico has protected nearly 11,000 acres along the Mimbres River as a new wildlife area, safeguarding historic water rights, rare river habitat and a 2-mile stretch of the desert stream
articles.summary: US News: Conservationists and state officials in New Mexico have completed a deal to buy nearly 11,000 acres of ecologically rich land along the Mimbres River,.
articles.body: Conservationists and state officials in New Mexico have completed a deal to buy nearly 11,000 acres of ecologically rich land along the Mimbres River, permanently protecting an important desert watershed and creating the state's newest public conservation preserve. The purchase secures the newly created Mimbres Ranch Wildlife Management Area (WMA), a large property bordering the Gila National Forest in southwestern New Mexico. The project was completed with help from the national non-profit Trust for Public Land (TPL) and the state government. The acquisition places about two miles of the Mimbres River under public ownership while protecting historic water rights that date back more than a century. The property also creates a large, connected area for native wildlife and expands public access along the scenic Trail of the Mountain Spirits Byway.Protecting water rights and desert habitatA key part of the deal is the permanent protection of important pre-1907 water rights connected to the Mimbres River. In the dry American Southwest, these water rights have major legal and environmental importance. They were established before New Mexico adopted its wider water code and have senior priority under state law. Protecting the rights will help keep water flowing through the river rather than being diverted for industrial or large-scale municipal use. This will support the river's surrounding riparian bosque, a green area of trees and plants that depends on the water. The Mimbres River is part of a rare closed-basin desert stream system. Its water stays within the basin instead of flowing into an ocean or another major river system. This unusual system has created a unique habitat for plants and animals adapted to the valley."At a time when public lands are under threat across the country, New Mexico is leaning in on conservation," said Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham in an official release published by the State of New Mexico Newsroom. "Protecting nearly 11,000 acres along the Mimbres River means healthier wildlife, cleaner water, and more places for New Mexico families to hunt, fish, and get outside. New Mexicans will benefit from this investment for generations to come."Protecting rare fish and wildlifeThe new wildlife management area contains a mix of Southwestern habitats, including high-desert grasslands, pinyon-juniper woodlands, cottonwood forests along the river and areas of ponderosa pine. These habitats support large animals such as Rocky Mountain elk, mule deer, black bears and mountain lions. They also provide habitat for birds including Merriam's turkey and quail. The property also contains designated critical habitat for federally protected species, including the western yellow-billed cuckoo and Chiricahua leopard frog. State fisheries biologists said the property is also important for protecting native fish found in the Mimbres drainage."This will create additional habitat for conserving the Rio Grande sucker and Chihuahua chub," said Kirk Patten, Chief of the Fisheries Management Division at the New Mexico Department of Game and Fish, in coverage reported by Organ Mountain News. "Both these fish are native to the Mimbres drainage, and this acquisition will ensure they continue to thrive there for years to come." The WMA will also connect with the Gila National Forest and existing protected areas, including The Nature Conservancy's Mimbres River Preserve. This will join previously separated habitats into a larger, more connected landscape.Broad support for the projectThe project received funding and legislative support through state conservation programmes, with environmental groups providing technical help. Representative Nathan Small, a Democrat from Las Cruces who supported funding for the project in the state legislature, highlighted the importance of the river and surrounding land. "Here in New Mexico, our land and water are sacred. The Mimbres River and its surrounding uplands vibrate with life, supporting hundreds of plant, animal, bird, and even rare fish species," Small stated in the official announcement published by Trust for Public Land. "The Mimbres Ranch WMA will enhance this ecosystem and create new recreation opportunities, including opportunities for New Mexico resident hunters." The property is also important for its history. It was once home to the ancient Mimbres culture, part of the Mogollon tradition and known for its distinctive black-on-white pottery made between about 1000 AD and 1150 AD.Jim Petterson, Mountain West Region Vice-President for the Trust for Public Land, said the purchase was the result of several years of cooperation between different groups. "This project represents a major win for wildlife, water and communities across New Mexico," said Petterson in an official press release. "By protecting this ecologically rich property, we are ensuring that this extraordinary landscape, home to rare species and critical waterways, will remain intact and accessible to the public for generations to come."State officials also described the acquisition as a long-term investment in conservation, tourism and outdoor recreation. "This acquisition represents an investment in the long-term sustainability of New Mexico's treasured wildlife, as well as its outdoor heritage," said Mike Sloane, Director of the New Mexico Department of Game and Fish, in statements carried by the Governor's Office. "Protecting this landscape helps conserve habitat for big game, native fish and other species, while creating new opportunities for the public to enjoy our state's outdoor spaces."Located near both the Gila Wilderness and the Aldo Leopold Wilderness, the Mimbres Ranch Wildlife Management Area is expected to eventually offer hiking, licensed seasonal hunting, horseback riding and bird watching. The New Mexico Department of Game and Fish said detailed management plans and rules for public access will be released after initial assessments of the property are completed.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Dolly Parton: A life in pictures
articles.summary: The singer rose from humble beginnings to become one of the most beloved entertainers in the world.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton, the country music superstar from the Smoky Mountains of Tennessee, rose from humble beginnings to become one of the most beloved entertainers in the world.

Over a career spanning more than 60 years, she sold more than 100 million records, wrote more than 3,000 songs and won 11 Grammy Awards, including a lifetime achievement honour.

Yet she has always described herself first and foremost as a songwriter. "It's my way of expressing myself. It's my therapy," she once said.

Dolly Parton grew up in poverty in a one-room cabin on the banks of the Little Pigeon River in Tennessee's Smoky Mountains, the fourth of 12 children.

She performed on local radio and television as a child and recorded her first single at 13.

After moving to Nashville the day after graduating from Sevier County High School, Dolly Parton scored her first solo hit with Dumb Blonde in 1966.

In 1967, country star Porter Wagoner invited Parton to join The Porter Wagoner Show, giving her a regular role on his nationally syndicated television programme as well as a place in his touring stage show.

Her breakthrough came with the album Hello, I'm Dolly.

Dolly Parton became a member of the Grand Ole Opry on January 4, 1969.

She has described the Opry as the "church of my heart" and said performing there was a lifelong dream.

In one remarkable 1973 writing session, Parton penned two of her signature hits – Jolene and I Will Always Love You.

Having written thousands of songs across her decades-long career, Parton said songwriting was her greatest form of self-expression.

Known for her larger-than-life image, Dolly Parton combined rhinestones, wit and charm to sustain a career that crossed from country to mainstream pop.

She headlined festivals and became a global star with albums such as Here You Come Again.

Parton also became known for memorable collaborations, notably with Kenny Rogers, whose duet Islands in the Stream became one of the defining hits of the 1980s.

While Dolly Parton is best known for her decades-spanning music career, her work as an actor has also left a lasting impression on film audiences.

Parton's breakout screen role came in the 1980 workplace comedy 9 to 5, where she starred alongside Jane Fonda, Lily Tomlin and Dabney Coleman.

Her portrayal of Doralee Rhodes combined comic timing with warmth, helping to redefine expectations of performers crossing over from music into film.

She followed this with roles in films such as The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas, alongside Burt Reynolds, and Steel Magnolias.

The latter featured an ensemble cast including Julia Roberts and Sally Field alongside Sylvester Stallone.

In these performances, Parton demonstrated a balance of humour and emotional depth, often anchoring scenes with a distinctly understated presence.

In 1986 Dolly Parton opened Dollywood, a theme park in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, near her birthplace.

It became a major tourist attraction - one of the most visited regional theme parks in the USA.

The park's success helped fund Parton's charitable foundation and literacy programme.

Through her Imagination Library, founded in honour of her father who could not read, Dolly Parton has given away more than 100 million free books to children around the world.

Her own book, Coat of Many Colours, was the 100 millionth book that programme donated to the US Library of Congress collection.

A council in Scotland announced it would dedicate a day to Dolly Parton every year to mark the impact of her reading scheme.

Parton personally donated millions to medical research and disaster relief.

The singer also led several major disaster-relief efforts, most notably creating the My People Fund after the 2016 Great Smoky Mountains wildfires which distributed about $10m to families who lost homes.

She lined up an all-star list of performers for a three-hour telethon to raise money.

In 2024, she pledged $2m for Hurricane Helene relief in East Tennessee and Appalachia, combining a personal donation with matching support from her businesses and foundation.

Parton's 2014 Glastonbury Festival appearance quickly became one of the defining "Legends" slot performances in the event's history.

Drawing one of the festival's biggest-ever daytime crowds - estimated at more than 180,000 - she turned the Pyramid Stage into a mass singalong, with renditions of Jolene, 9 to 5 and I Will Always Love You prompting scenes of near-universal audience participation.

In 2019, Parton celebrated 50 years as an Opry member with a major televised special called Dolly Parton: 50 Years at the Opry.

The event featured performances and tributes from other country artists.

Her decades-spanning relationship with the Opry helped cement its status as both a guardian of country music tradition and a stage for modern stars.

Parton gradually began to step away from major touring, saying she no longer wanted to spend long stretches on the road.

Instead, she focused on selective live shows, new recording projects and screen appearances including Dolly Parton's Heartstrings, Mountain Magic and Christmas on the Square for Netflix.

In 2021, Parton publicly received a Covid-19 vaccine at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, using the moment to encourage others to do the same.

She sang an adapted version of her hit Jolene, singing: "Vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, I'm begging of you, please don't hesitate."

Parton's 2022 induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame marked a characteristically self-aware turn.

Having initially said she had not "earned" the honour, she later embraced it with humour - declaring "I'm a rock star now" - before performing her new song Rockin', written especially for the ceremony, a symbolic step toward her later rock album Rockstar.

In 2023, Parton delivered another headline-grabbing live moment when she performed at the Dallas Cowboys' Thanksgiving halftime show, appearing in a rhinestone-studded Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders outfit.

More recently, Parton continued to balance personal loss with new creative work.

Following the death of her husband Carl Dean in 2025, she released If You Hadn't Been There in tribute, while also continuing development of Dolly: A True Original Musical, the stage production based on her life and career.

In early 2026, Parton gave a pre-recorded tribute speech for Ozzy Osbourne at the BRIT Awards in Manchester, where Ozzy received a posthumous Lifetime Achievement Award.

Her speech was short but was one of the emotional highlights of the ceremony.

Parton had been due to return to the stage for a short Las Vegas residency, but announced this month that she was cancelling the run because of health issues, telling fans she needed "a little more time to heal".

She will remain a cultural icon remembered for her generosity and humour, as well as her extraordinary songwriting - the craft at the heart of a catalogue that has shaped modern country music and crossed generations.

It became a major tourist attraction - one of the most visited regional theme parks in the USA.
The park's success helped fund Parton's charitable foundation and literacy programme.
Through her Imagination Library, founded in honour of her father who could not read, Dolly Parton has given away more than 100 million free books to children around the world.
Her own book, Coat of Many Colours, was the 100 millionth book that programme donated to the US Library of Congress collection.
A council in Scotland announced it would dedicate a day to Dolly Parton every year to mark the impact of her reading scheme.
Parton personally donated millions to medical research and disaster relief.

The singer also led several major disaster-relief efforts, most notably creating the My People Fund after the 2016 Great Smoky Mountains wildfires which distributed about $10m to families who lost homes.
She lined up an all-star list of performers for a three-hour telethon to raise money.
In 2024, she pledged $2m for Hurricane Helene relief in East Tennessee and Appalachia, combining a personal donation with matching support from her businesses and foundation.
Parton's 2014 Glastonbury Festival appearance quickly became one of the defining "Legends" slot performances in the event's history.

Drawing one of the festival's biggest-ever daytime crowds - estimated at more than 180,000 - she turned the Pyramid Stage into a mass singalong, with renditions of Jolene, 9 to 5 and I Will Always Love You prompting scenes of near-universal audience participation.
In 2019, Parton celebrated 50 years as an Opry member with a major televised special called Dolly Parton: 50 Years at the Opry.
The event featured performances and tributes from other country artists.
Her decades-spanning relationship with the Opry helped cement its status as both a guardian of country music tradition and a stage for modern stars.
Parton gradually began to step away from major touring, saying she no longer wanted to spend long stretches on the road.
Instead, she focused on selective live shows, new recording projects and screen appearances including Dolly Parton's Heartstrings, Mountain Magic and Christmas on the Square for Netflix.
In 2021, Parton publicly received a Covid-19 vaccine at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, using the moment to encourage others to do the same.
She sang an adapted version of her hit Jolene, singing: "Vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, I'm begging of you, please don't hesitate."
Parton's 2022 induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame marked a characteristically self-aware turn.

Having initially said she had not "earned" the honour, she later embraced it with humour - declaring "I'm a rock star now" - before performing her new song Rockin', written especially for the ceremony, a symbolic step toward her later rock album Rockstar.

In 2023, Parton delivered another headline-grabbing live moment when she performed at the Dallas Cowboys' Thanksgiving halftime show, appearing in a rhinestone-studded Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders outfit.
More recently, Parton continued to balance personal loss with new creative work.

Following the death of her husband Carl Dean in 2025, she released If You Hadn't Been There in tribute, while also continuing development of Dolly: A True Original Musical, the stage production based on her life and career.
In early 2026, Parton gave a pre-recorded tribute speech for Ozzy Osbourne at the BRIT Awards in Manchester, where Ozzy received a posthumous Lifetime Achievement Award.
Her speech was short but was one of the emotional highlights of the ceremony.

Parton had been due to return to the stage for a short Las Vegas residency, but announced this month that she was cancelling the run because of health issues, telling fans she needed "a little more time to heal".

She will remain a cultural icon remembered for her generosity and humour, as well as her extraordinary songwriting - the craft at the heart of a catalogue that has shaped modern country music and crossed generations.

articles.title: China hits out at 'illegal' new US sanctions on Iran and trading partners
articles.summary: The US has threatened to isolate nations that continue to do business with Tehran, which sells much of its oil to Beijing.
articles.body:
Watch: What are these sanctions and who will be affected?

China has vowed to protect its interests after the US announced plans to widen economic sanctions against Iran and its trading partners, which include Beijing.

Foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said China was firmly opposed to what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights.

This came after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the new measures on Monday, warning any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.

China is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, although the trade has declined under the US blockade of Iran's ports.

Lin said: "Cooperation between China and Iran has always been conducted within the framework of international law and should not be interfered with or disrupted."

Bessent described the plans for sanctions as "the single greatest financial offensive ever" against Iran, warning banks and businesses would share in Iran's isolation if they refused to cut ties with the country.

He declined to focus on specific nations, but said US President Donald Trump would be phoning world leaders "with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime".

However, responding to a question about Chinese banks, Bessent said he wanted to make clear "no one was above the reach of US sanctions".

The announcement comes ahead of planned talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month.

Washington is likely to be wary of potential retaliation from Beijing, which processes the majority of the world's rare earths and other critical minerals, crucial in the manufacture of many high-tech products.

Beijing has already tightened export controls on rare earths as part of previous trade negotiations with the US.

China's response followed Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh saying Tehran was "fully prepared" for the wider sanctions, which he said would lead to "another defeat" for the US.

"The government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," he told state television.

"We also have our own tools and know how to play the game," he said, adding Tehran had been "waiting for these plans for a long time".

Iran says it is 'fully prepared' to counter widened US economic sanctions

The US has dubbed its latest sanctions "Operation Economic Outcast" and described them as an "economic D-Day" against Iran.

It comes almost six months after the start of the Iran war.

The conflict has since led to hikes in oil prices worldwide, with Tehran effectively blocking exports through the Strait of Hormuz - a waterway vital to the global economy. The US has also slowed traffic via its own naval blockade.

Recent attempts to end the conflict via diplomacy have failed, and a 60-day ceasefire formally expired last week with no sign of a settlement.

With the announcement of new sanctions, the US treasury secretary claimed America was "no longer managing the Iranian threat, we are ending it".

UK Chancellor John Healey said the British government supported "US work to secure a diplomatic solution and welcome efforts to increase pressure".

Iran is already under heavy sanctions from the US, but Bessent said these go further.

He said the Treasury had mapped financial channels, facilitators and networks used by Iran to evade sanctions to trade oil, imposing sanctions on almost 60 entities, individuals and vessels.

But analysts had cast doubt on the latest measures even before China's response.

David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, told the BBC the direct impact on Iran's energy revenues would be "somewhat of a damp squib".

"We suspect that the new package will have only a limited direct impact on Iranian energy flows in the short term," he added.

This is partly due to the fact roughly 90% of Iran's oil goes to China, he said, "which has not recognised US sanctions in the past and is unlikely to be cowed this time either".

Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa Program at the International Crisis Group, said: "Generally, the Chinese are against unilateral sanctions. They would comply with multilateral or international sanctions, but unilateral sanctions just imposed by the US - they have always seen that as illegitimate."

And although Iran's neighbours like Pakistan, Turkey and Iraq want to maintain good relationships with the US, they "can't really afford to cut off ties with Iran", Vaez told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

He said putting economic pressure on Tehran "doesn't work" because the Iranian regime is willing to "absorb any pain" and pass it onto the people.

Other trade partners that could be affected by the US announcement include India and Russia, who have not yet responded.

articles.title: India police clash with protesters a month after Gen Z demonstrations
articles.summary: Police used water cannons and batons as a few thousand protesters broke through security barricades in Bihar’s capital.
articles.body:
Indian students and unemployed youth have clashed with police as they marched towards the residence of the chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar, ruled by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party, demanding access to jobs and transparency in recruitment exams.

The government forces in Bihar used water cannons and lathis – the Indian version of batons – as a few thousand protesters broke through security barricades in the state capital Patna, videos seen by Al Jazeera showed on Tuesday.

The demonstrations came a month after massive Gen Z protests in New Delhi pushed for the ouster of India's education minister over alleged irregularities in conducting key competitive examinations.

The July 25 resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan also marked a significant political defeat for PM Modi, who has tried to maintain a strongman image , while India has continued to slide in multiple democratic indices under his rule since 2014.

Police in Bihar, home to about 130 million people, detained at least 25 protesters in Patna and released them later, according to the Indian Express newspaper.

Local police accused some protesters of attacking security personnel.

"Police will identify those involved in stone pelting at police and will take action against them," Patna Police Superintendent Kartikeya K Sharma told reporters on Tuesday.

The protests began last week with unemployed youth demanding jobs, but they later expanded to include calls for education reform .

Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary said his office was "listening to every student's voice".

A delegation of student representatives met Bihar's top bureaucrat, Pratyaya Amrit, after the protests. Amrit then told reporters that the discussion "was positive, and we were assured of a favourable response within a couple of days".

The tight employment market in India makes government jobs, which offer long-term stability, a major draw for millions.

Since the massive youth-led protests organised by the online Cockroach Janta Party in New Delhi, there have been similar demonstrations in other states challenging both the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and opposition parties.

In southern Karnataka, members of a BJP-linked student body staged a protest near the state chief minister's residence on Tuesday over alleged irregularities in recruitment for government jobs.

Bihar's regional Education Minister Mithilesh Tiwari said the government had addressed students' demands, without giving more details, and added that the door for dialogue remained "wide open".

In New Delhi, the Cockroach movement has also announced a march next month to protest against what it says is the Modi government's failure to fulfil several promises of change , including the withdrawal of police cases against protesters.

articles.title: Brazil fines TikTok $30 mn in 'powerful signal' over child safety
articles.summary: Brazil's data protection agency on Tuesday fined TikTok nearly $30 million for failing to implement child safety measures in what it said was a "powerful sig...
articles.body:
Brazil's data protection agency on Tuesday fined TikTok nearly $30 million for failing to implement child safety measures in what it said was a "powerful signal" to social media companies.

Brazil has taken a tough stance on the regulation of social media platforms, cracking down on disinformation and requiring users under 16 to have their accounts linked to those of their parents.

Fabricio Lopes, an enforcement director with the ANPD data protection agency, told a press conference that TikTok "was not taking the necessary measures to prevent adolescents from accessing the platform and from having the data of these children and adolescents processed."

This data was "being used to offer advertising to adolescents."

He said the fine of 153.7 million reais ($29.9 million) was a "powerful signal to other platforms regarding how seriously the ANPD takes this work" and that the agency hoped they would "get the message."

TikTok agreed last week to pay $400 million to settle a lawsuit with the US Department of Justice over claims that the video-sharing platform collected children's personal data without parental permission.

The ANPD this month also ordered popular streaming platform Discord to suspend livestreams and video calls after a teenage girl was allegedly encouraged to take her own life during a broadcast.

The agency told AFP that an appeal filed by Discord on Monday against the suspension is under review.

ANPD director Lorena Giuberti Coutinho said the agency had last week initiated proceedings to verify the compliance of 22 social media networks and platforms with a law passed this year to protect children and teens online.

"I think we can expect much stronger enforcement action" in coming months, she said.

In addition to the fine, the ANPD ordered TikTok parent company ByteDance to delete data collected in violation of regulations.

Coutinho said TikTok had committed to suspending all advertisements for users who are not logged in.

TikTok has committed to "implementing a compliance plan to improve the protection of children and adolescents," the ANPD said.

The platform will be required to automatically apply stricter privacy settings to accounts belonging to children under the age of 16, strengthen parental supervision systems, and implement stricter content filters.

In a statement sent to AFP, TikTok said the fine stems from concerns raised in 2021 and "does not take into account" measures that have been implemented since then.

The statement said TikTok has rolled out over 50 safety features aimed at teens over the past six years.

These include restricting direct messaging for children under 16, not recommending this age group's content to strangers, and allowing parents to set screen-time limits and block accounts.

According to the ANPD, TikTok has ten days to appeal the fine.

In 2024, the platform X was blocked for 40 days in Brazil until the social media network owned by the world's richest person, Elon Musk, complied with the Supreme Court's orders to remove accounts spreading disinformation.

articles.title: How Nathan Straus transformed philanthropy and helped make pasteurised milk the safer choice for children
articles.summary: US News: Long before pasteurised milk became a routine part of American life, families in New York faced a serious and often overlooked public-health danger, c.
articles.body: Long before pasteurised milk became a routine part of American life, families in New York faced a serious and often overlooked public-health danger, contaminated milk. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, raw milk could carry harmful pathogens and was especially dangerous for infants and young children. One wealthy businessman, Nathan Straus, used his fortune and business experience to tackle the problem in an unconventional way. Rather than simply donating money to charities, Straus created a system that combined philanthropy with practical retail distribution. He established milk laboratories and depots where pasteurised and refrigerated milk could be sold cheaply or provided free to families who could not afford it. His campaign eventually helped push pasteurisation into mainstream public-health policy and left a lasting mark on how Americans understood safe milk.Nathan Straus turned his business experience towards philanthropyNathan Straus was born in 1848 and became wealthy through his involvement with major New York department stores, including Abraham and Straus and R.H. Macy and Co. After building his fortune, he and his wife, Lina Gutherz Straus, increasingly devoted their attention to philanthropic causes. The New York Public Libraryâs papers document his work in public health, milk pasteurisation, tuberculosis prevention and assistance to people affected by poverty and disasters. Strausâs approach to charity differed from the traditional model of simply handing out money. During the economic depression of the 1890s, he used his experience in merchandising to establish depots near New Yorkâs poorer neighbourhoods, where essential goods could be provided at reduced prices. This practical approach later shaped his campaign for safer milk. His interest in milk became particularly personal and urgent. At the time, milk could spoil during transportation and storage, while contaminated supplies could expose children to dangerous diseases. Straus believed that improving the way milk was processed and distributed could save lives.The milk crisis that put children at riskIn New York City during the 1890s, infant mortality was extraordinarily high. Raw milk was considered one of the major risks because it could contain disease-causing organisms, including bacteria associated with tuberculosis. Although scientists already understood that heating milk could destroy harmful microorganisms, pasteurisation was not yet universally accepted. Straus became one of its most determined advocates. In 1892, he established the Nathan Straus Pasteurized Milk Laboratory in New York at his own expense.
