articles.title: Trump administration plans mass visa revocations for people seeking asylum
articles.summary: A sweeping new effort would affect people who entered the U.S. as temporary visitors before seeking asylum, further narrowing access to protection.
articles.body:
The Trump administration plans to revoke visas from people who entered the United States legally as tourists or business travelers and later applied for asylum – opening a new front in its campaign to restrict access to humanitarian protection.

The Department of State is coordinating with the Department of Homeland Security to identify people who arrived on B-1 or B-2 visas and subsequently sought asylum in a move aimed at "making clear that a visa is a privilege – not a right," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a statement to USA TODAY.

"These types of visas are issued with the clear understanding that they are for those who intend to return home," Pigott added. "Obtaining a visa in order to seek asylum is fraud – which is grounds for visa revocation. This is an ongoing process as we uphold the integrity of our visa and asylum laws."

The State Department has not explained how it will determine whether people obtained a visa intending to apply for asylum. It also hasn't detailed how it will figure out whether visa-holders decided to seek protection later because conditions in their home countries or their personal circumstances changed. Pigott also did not specify how many people would be affected, saying the number of revocations "remains dynamic" and that they would occur on a rolling basis.

The Associated Press, which first reported the administration's plans, said as many as 200,000 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 could be revoked, citing State Department documents and two U.S. officials. If carried out on that scale, according to the AP, it would be the largest single mass visa revocation in U.S. history.

When Luis and his mother fled Venezuela in 2017, they boarded a flight to Florida with visitor visas in hand. Luis, whom USA TODAY is identifying only by his first name because he fears that speaking publicly could jeopardize his asylum case, said they were determined to follow the law even as they sought safety.

Luis, 26, said he had been wounded and threatened by security officials amid the Venezuelan government's violent crackdown on protests, in which scores of people were killed. Soon after arriving, Luis and his mother applied for asylum, believing they had done "everything by the book," he said. Then they waited. Nearly nine years later, his case remains unresolved.

"And there's nothing I can do until USCIS moves my case," he said. "This is out of my hands, and, trust me, if I could, I would choose anything over this anxiety-inducing waiting game. But going home is simply not an option."

Now, Luis fears the path he chose because he believed it was legal could be used as evidence that he broke the law – and that his request for protection could make him a target.

It remains unclear what the revocation plans would mean for Luis or others with pending asylum claims. However, experts said revoking a visa alone may have little impact on someone already in the country. A visa allows a foreign national to travel to a U.S. port of entry and request admission; revoking it would generally prevent the person from using it to return to the U.S., but would not, on its own, cancel a pending asylum application.

"The action has very little effect," said David Bier, director of immigration studies at the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank.

The move could carry greater consequences, if DHS separately cancels any immigration status the person holds, he said, potentially exposing some applicants to arrest by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Neither agency has said whether the revocations will be accompanied by changes to applicants' immigration status, formal fraud findings, removal proceedings or other enforcement actions. When reached for comment, DHS referred USA TODAY to the State Department.

Dara Lind, a senior fellow at the American Immigration Council – an immigrant rights groups – said the practical reach may be smaller than the figure reported by the AP suggests. Some visas issued as far back as 2016 may have expired, she said, and it is unclear how many people would lose an immigration status on which they still rely. The announcement, she said, may function partly as a "scare tactic," sowing fear among asylum seekers, even if its immediate legal consequences remain limited.

"It's not super clear where on the scale of saber-rattling – just declaring that they don't like things – versus actually materially changing a lot of people's circumstances this particular thing is," she said.

But Lind said the initiative sends a broader message about the administration's efforts to make seeking asylum increasingly untenable.

"What is the right way to apply for asylum in the U.S. right now, according to the Trump administration?" Lind said.

Applying affirmatively through USCIS has traditionally been regarded as a lawful way to seek protection, she said, yet the administration is now seeking to penalize some immigrants for doing precisely that.

"It's another kind of demonstration that they are doing everything they can to keep applying for asylum from being something that allows you to stay in the United States," Lind said.

Rooted in international protections developed after World War II, the modern U.S. asylum system was established through the Refugee Act of 1980. It allows people facing persecution because of their race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership in a particular social group to seek protection. Under federal law, a person must be physically present in the United States or arriving at its border to apply for asylum. The law allows people to seek that protection regardless of their immigration status.

But the visa initiative follows years of mounting political tension over asylum, particularly after the U.S. experienced historically high levels of migration at the southern border during the Biden administration. Many of those arriving sought asylum, putting pressure on a system that has been backlogged for a decade and fueling criticism that applicants could remain in the country for years while their cases were decided.

Administration officials have pointed to those concerns to justify the new visa crackdown.

"People in the US and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims," Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau wrote Monday on X. "Asylum isn't supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration law."

President Joe Biden imposed his own restrictions on asylum access in 2024 as border crossings became a defining political vulnerability. Donald Trump campaigned on going much further, promising to halt illegal immigration and carry out mass deportations.

Since last year, Trump has pursued a series of actions intended to restrict access to asylum and accelerate removals. On his first day back in office, he issued a proclamation declaring crossings at the southern border an "invasion" and sought to prevent many immigrants arriving there from applying for asylum.

In April, a federal appeals court ruled that the administration could not categorically bar people already in the country from applying for asylum or circumvent the removal procedures established by Congress. Federal law, the court wrote , gives people physically present in the United States a right to apply, regardless of their status or whether they arrived at an official port of entry.

By the end of fiscal 2025, more than 1.4 million affirmative asylum applications were pending before U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, according to DHS . Separately, about 2.3 million people with formal asylum applications were awaiting hearings or decisions in immigration court as of June, according to data from the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse , a nonprofit data gathering organization at Syracuse University.

A pending asylum application does not itself confer lawful immigration status or prevent someone from being placed in removal proceedings. Still, asylum seekers were generally allowed to remain in the country while their claims were adjudicated and, after meeting eligibility requirements, could obtain authorization to work. Under previous administrations, applicants without criminal records were typically not prioritized for arrest or detention.

That has changed under Trump. Federal immigration agents have detained people with pending claims at immigration courthouses and during routine ICE check-ins – appointments they were required to attend as part of their cases.

The administration has also reshaped the courts deciding many asylum cases. The Justice Department has fired immigration judges , appointed some military lawyers to serve as temporary immigration judges and increasingly turned to mass hearings as it seeks to push cases through more quickly.

Though asylum denial rates had been slowly rising since late 2023, they have surged under Trump, TRAC data shows . In September 2023, fewer than half of applicants were denied. By June 2026, the latest month available, the denial rate had reached 94.1 percent.

Lind said the government is increasingly targeting immigrants who have spent years complying with its requirements – filing applications, renewing work permits, paying fees and reporting changes of address – only to remain trapped in a backlog they cannot control.

"You don't need to know the ins and outs of immigration law to know that so many of the people who have been most harmed by this administration are people who have spent years of their lives making sure that they check all the boxes, dot all the i's and cross all the t's," she said.

"None of these people would have pending applications if USCIS were processing applications in a timely fashion," Lind added. "Instead of actually putting any effort toward adjudicating those cases, they're doing all of these things that are punishing the people who have been waiting in line."

The crackdown on asylum seekers comes as the U.S. government has also made it more difficult and expensive to enter or remain in the country through legal channels.

The State Department said this month that it had revoked more than 175,000 visas since Trump returned to office, mostly following law enforcement encounters. Other revocations involved alleged visa violations, fraud, calls for violence or national security threats. The administration has expanded social media screening, targeted foreign students accused of antisemitic activity and revoked more than 600 visas through a task force focused on alleged "birth tourism."

It has also required a $100,000 payment for certain new work visa petitions and moved to limit how long foreign students, exchange visitors and journalists may remain in the country.

For nearly nine years, Luis said, he has renewed his work permit, complied with the government's requirements and waited for it to decide whether he can remain in the country where he sought refuge.

He thought entering with a visa and applying through the asylum system meant he was following the rules. Now, he said, doing everything the government asked of him has not made him feel safe.

"It feels like you're being hunted," Luis said. "And my only 'crime' is seeking the American dream."

articles.title: A Virginia university fought against its first gay student group — and lost. Now it’s honoring them
articles.summary: Virginia Commonwealth University will unveil a historical marker honoring the students whose landmark court victory expanded constitutional protections for L...
articles.body:
Virginia Commonwealth University leaders tried more than 50 years ago to prevent the formation of their school's first gay student group. Now, the organization's history will be honored with a historical marker.

VCU will unveil the commemorative marker on campus in October, according to Richmond ABC affiliate WRIC . It will recount the history of VCU's Gay Alliance of Students, which was founded in 1974. The university initially rejected the organization's application for official recognition, leading to a two-year court battle that ended with a federal appeals court ruling that the school had violated the students' constitutional rights.

The landmark Gay Alliance of Students v. Matthews decision opened the door for similar student organizations at colleges and universities throughout the federal judicial circuit that includes Virginia, Maryland , North Carolina , South Carolina and West Virginia . The organization has celebrated the 50th anniversary of its court victory throughout the last year.

Related : Emails reveal Virginia school officials approved an LGBTQ+ club — until conservative backlash hit

The commemoration will culminate with a gala and an October 16 unveiling of the historical marker, whose text has been approved by the Virginia Department of Historic Resources:

"A group of students at Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU) in Richmond established in September 1974 the Gay Alliance of Students, the university's first openly LGBTQ+ student organization. A legal battle that attracted local and national support for the Alliance ensued after VCU rejected its application for official recognition. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit ruled in Gay Alliance of Students v. Matthews in October 1976 that VCU's refusal to recognize the organization violated the First and Fourteenth Amendments of the U.S. Constitution. The court's decision set a legal precedent. It extended protections to similar student groups in Virginia, Maryland, North Carolina, South Carolina, and West Virginia."

Related : A rural Virginia school board changed its rules to block an LGBTQ+ club. Students are suing in federal court

The half-century-old fight echoes today in another federal courtroom in Richmond. Two students and their families sued the King George County School Board this month after officials blocked a proposed Gay-Straight Alliance at King George Middle School while continuing to allow other noncurricular groups.

The lawsuit alleges that officials repeatedly changed the rules in response to opposition to the GSA, violating the students' First Amendment rights and the federal Equal Access Act. The families are asking a judge to order the district to allow the organization to operate on the same terms as other student groups.

Related : A Virginia school board bent over backward to block an LGBTQ+ club. One mom explains why she's suing

University officials hope the marker will signal that VCU welcomes everyone — decades after its leaders tried to deny LGBTQ+ students official representation.

"I hope that when students and alumni see this marker, they understand that VCU is for everyone, and that students' voices and alumni voices matter," said Josh Leidy, director of affinity programs in VCU's Office of Development and Alumni Relations, in a statement released by VCU . "The Gay Alliance of Students case only came about because students had the courage to stand up and advocate for what needed to happen for the community."

articles.title: Chinese teens are turning to mind-numbing drugs to 'run away from reality'
articles.summary: Students are seeking prescription drugs because they fear failure, a teen tells the BBC.
articles.body:
At 14, *Xiaomei, a high-performing student from a coastal province in China, decided to overdose on cough medication.

She wanted to impress an older boy who told her it would help her relax. The tablets were usually only available with a doctor's prescription, but she managed to buy them online.

At first she found that they made her a bit dizzy. But she was soon hooked to the slightly numb sensation, which, to her, felt like a brief respite from the pressure of looming exams. When taken in large doses, the drug can cause serious side effects, including hallucinations and impaired coordination.

Eventually she tried other medication recommended to her on chat groups. Some were for pain or epileptic seizures. Sometimes she would take five tablets. Other times she would try more than 10 to feel the effects of different drugs.

For two years, she took large quantities of various prescription drugs. None of them were prescribed to her or anyone in her family. She bought them all on the internet.

"When I felt too much pressure from my studies, or I didn't do well at exams, or even when I quarrelled with my parents, I would take these drugs," she told the BBC. "I was running away from reality."

The BBC has heard similar stories from dozens of Chinese teenagers in chat rooms across various social media platforms. Nearly every one of them seemed to be escaping the same thing: pressure. They were doing that by chasing what is being described as a "pharmaceutical high".

One girl shared a voice note after taking large doses of a neuropathic pain drug. Her words were slurred and hard to comprehend: "I feel my body doesn't belong to me. I'm so dizzy."

“Just sleep," comes the advice. "You will be fine tomorrow."

One boy offered to use his father's old prescription to fake a new one for the same drug.

Some offered tips: "If you want to hallucinate, you can just buy... it's not been controlled yet," says one user, suggesting a drug used by people with Parkinson's to control tremors. In excessive doses it can cause confusion or even delirium.

"Which keyword should I use to search for it on online platforms," another user asks.

It is hard to gauge the scale of the problem, as there are few official figures.

But it is serious enough that the government launched a nationwide crackdown two years ago against the cough suppressant Xiaomei started using, classifying it as a psychotropic drug which would only be available to patients with a doctor's prescription. That made it much harder for young people to buy online.

Then in April this year, authorities noticed that young people had switched to another drug and imposed tighter controls on how it is prescribed and dispensed at chemists. Still the BBC was offered the drug in an online chat room for as little as 10 Chinese yuan ($1.5; £1.09) per gram.

"Non-regulated substances are easy to acquire and even when one drug is controlled by the authorities, young people quickly find alternatives," says a 2025 paper written for the Crime Prevention Institute at the Ministry of Justice.

In some cases the BBC found that teens online were using different names for drugs to avoid detection, which the 2025 study also noted.

There is growing evidence that young people across the world are turning to prescription medication to fight off pressures and anxiety .

So easy access to cheap prescription drugs in China is perhaps not that surprising given that it produces the vast majority of the world's pharmaceutical ingredients.

When Xiaomei wanted to buy the cough suppressant, it just took a few clicks for an entire box of the medication to be delivered at her door, she says. "You could simply enter your ID number on shopping platforms and buy it directly."

The ID, which is a national identity number, includes her age but she says she was still sold the drug, no questions asked. It was also cheap - often 50 tablets cost less than a dollar.

On paper, China is winning the war on illegal drugs. Official data for 2025 shows a dramatic fall - 41% - in newly identified drug users under the age of 35.

However authorities have had to acknowledge that the misuse of prescription drugs is becoming a widespread problem. It has been especially surging among minors, China's National Narcotics Control Commission warned in a recent report.

Xiaomei says that a lot of students in her elite chemistry class were discussing ways to overdose on prescription drugs to avoid feeling like "complete losers".

"It is just so hard to pass exams and to stay in elite classes. In our school, the elite classes operate on an elimination system; if your academic scores drop, you get kicked out of the class. When you fail, you feel like failures, believing you have no chance in life."

Part of the pressure comes from parents who also see their child as their only hope for the future, says renowned Chinese sociologist and director of the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology, Xiang Biao.

Because of the one-child policy which ended in 2016 after decades, many families only have one child, Biao adds, who shoulders all their expectations.

"What makes Chinese teens different is their isolating environment. They spend at least nine or 10 hours in school. They have very few chances to develop social relationships, very few opportunities to witness what life is really like."

More worrying, he sees a link between prescription drug abuse and an increase in self-harm. The BBC noticed, for instance, that in many of the chat rooms, young people would encourage one another to cut themselves "to feel something".

As an extremely competitive high school entrance exam drew close, Xiaomei tried a different drug, searching for ways to numb the anxiety.

"But my memory deteriorated rapidly," she says. "I couldn't remember anything clearly, and I lived in a constant daze."

The drug is usually prescribed to help control epileptic seizures and it works as neuropathic pain medication. When Xiaomei explained the side effects in one of her chat groups, they suggested another drug, which is given as pain relief. She says it gave her some release but she soon needed higher doses.

Months before sitting the important exam, she went too far.

She'd taken 50 tablets and started to panic. "I was afraid something serious might happen, but I didn't want to have my stomach pumped so I wanted to wait before telling my parents."

But she became so unwell that she had to confess.

Her parents decided to listen to what they saw as their daughter's cry for help.

"They mostly expressed how heartbreaking it was for them to see me like that. They didn't scold or criticise me. Their approach was gentle."

For her, this has made all the difference.

"Many children receive lots of attention but the type of attention they want is to be asked how they feel. Do they feel lonely or stressed? Often in China parents brush that away and say you just have to be stronger," Biao says.

"There's a very loud alarm being sounded out across Chinese society. Adults have to examine how to be responsible for a teenager. Having an open conversation as a family - that is probably the most rewarding part of life."

And that is where the real battle lies, according to experts. Rather than playing whack-a-mole trying to suppress online sales of prescription drugs, the government should focus on what may well be a mental health crisis, they say.

In 2023, a study for China's Mental Health Blue Book found that nearly 95 million people suffer from depression and more than 30% were under 18 years old.

The Chinese government has recognised the need for mental health support for teens. Those plans include counselling rooms in every school, psychiatric services in at least one hospital in every county and more mental health professionals. The aim is to build a nationwide system of psychological support and crisis intervention by 2030.

So far they have been quite successful. According to the State Council, 92% of primary schools and 95% of junior middle schools now have a counsellor. Many major cities, including Beijing, have started to incorporate mental health into the curriculum.

However, there is still a major shortage of medical psychiatrists specialising in children and adolescents.

A 2020 study published in British medical journal The Lancet claimed there were only 500 qualified child psychiatrists in the country, and many of them were based in major cities such as Beijing and Shanghai.

This is a huge challenge in a country that has undergone three decades of unprecedented social and economic change.

The China Xiaomei's parents grew up in is very different from the future she is facing. Her parents followed a script set by the Communist Party: work hard and you will be rewarded. Now, even if young adults pass with high grades and get a university degree, a bright future is not guaranteed.

Following gruelling pandemic restrictions, the Chinese economy has struggled to bounce back. One in five young people are thought to be struggling to find a job and families are spending less.

"People have become more pessimistic in general," Biao admits. And the anxiety extends to adults, he adds.

"I think parents feel confused and anxious because they see a problem in their children, but they don't see an alternative. If my child has a problem, it's the end of the world. If my child doesn't do well in school, it's the end of the world. If my child doesn't speak to me, it's the end of the world. I think we should pay more attention to parents as well as children."

Fortunately Xiaomei and her parents have managed to find a way to cross this bridge.

"In the past, my parents didn't really understand me and would say some pretty harsh things. I felt like I had no help and was truly on my own," she says.

But that changed when she was rushed to hospital after the overdose. They started listening to her and talking to her, and "knowing that there was someone standing by my side made me feel really good", she says. It even helped her perform well in the entrance exam she had been dreading for so long.

"I am lucky to have their support," she adds.

Not everyone finds such support though, and that's where *Lu Jingchan hopes he can help.

The 22-year-old spent years battling depression. He found it hard to beat the euphoria that came from taking prescription drugs, and overdosed more than four times in four years.

"The drugs drove me to the brink of madness. You risk sinking into an abyss of addiction, destroying your health," he says.

He has now quit all prescription medication, and spends his time on social media urging others not to start. And he has this advice for young people battling the pressures he once did.

"I hope you can face life head-on, without needing medicines to numb yourselves. If you are overdosing, I want to give you the courage to stop. I believe your lives will improve. I believe you will all find happiness."

* Names have been changed to protect their identity

articles.title: Man kills eight relatives, including children, in shooting at Montana home, officials say
articles.summary: Home in Billings was also set on fire, with victims representing four generations of a blended family
articles.body:
A man killed eight of his relatives, including four children, on Sunday evening in a shooting at a home in Billings, Montana , that was also set on fire, according to authorities and local media reports.

Police have characterized the case as a family disturbance, according to Montana news outlet KULR .

The victims represented four generations of the blended family, ranging from a great-grandmother in her nineties to a seven-year-old girl, according to Jennifer Mercer, a neighbor and family friend who set up an online fundraiser to help cover funeral costs and other expenses and was authorized to release those details.

The suspect in the case was found outside the home with a self-inflicted gunshot wound, police said. He was taken to hospital, where he later died.

Brad Ireland, whose former wife and two children were among the dead, identified the shooter as Alan Smith, 44. Smith had recently been told to move out of the home, Ireland said.

An officer responded to a call reporting a shooter at a home in Billings's west end area at about 6pm, the city's police department said . The officer heard gunshots fired from the back of the house arriving and then saw the home fully engulfed in flames.

The local Yellowstone county sheriff, Kent O'Donnell, told a news conference on Monday that all victims targeted in the shooting were dead – with "multiple adults and multiple juveniles" killed.

Firefighters were dispatched but had to wait until officers had secured the scene – and they also may have faced water access issues, officials said. "The delay in limited access presented significant challenges, fire conditions continued to worsen and the residents ultimately became … consumed by fire," Matt Hoppel, the Billings fire chief said at Monday's news conference.

O'Donnell added: "Because of the fire and obviously water that goes to suppress that fire, it's going to slow our investigation of the crime scene recovery of evidence. So we ask for patience as we complete this investigation."

Details about a motive were not immediately released, and neither was an explanation for how the fire was started. Authorities have asked the public to avoid the scene as investigators continue to collect evidence, and they expected to provide another update on Wednesday.

A statement from Billings police Sgt Jeff Stovall extended condolences "to everyone affected by this awful tragedy" while adding that authorities were intentionally limiting details about the case "to protect the integrity of the ongoing investigation".

The killings in Montana came after five people were killed in rural Forest Grove, Oregon , by a man who then evidently died by suicide, according to authorities.

Authorities on Tuesday identified the victims in that case as Mary Elizabeth Kimsey, 85; Rowan Karla Kimsey, 60; Stella Jade Kimsey, 26; Linsey Mae Haraldsen, 26; and Alvin Raymond Chu, 27, according to the local Washington county sheriff's office.

Their suspected killer was Benjamin C Parker, 36, who was the partner of Stella Kimsey, officials said. Rowan and Mary Kimsey were Stella's mother and grandmother, respectively, they said.

The killings in Oregon pushed the number of mass murders in the US for the year so far to at least 16, according to information from the Gun Violence Archive, a nonpartisan resource. If the number of victims in the Montana case is verified, that number would increase to 17 – including five in August alone.

The archive defines a mass murder as cases in which four or more victims are killed.

A substantial number of mass murders in the US fit the definition of a crime known as a family annihilation. That crime involves the killings of multiple close family members, most commonly by an armed male.

US communities have historically perceived family annihilations in isolation. But a July 2023 Indianapolis Star investigation found they were occurring across the US every five days on average – and raised questions about why the country has not sought a nationwide strategy to mitigate the frequency of that particular type of crime.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Warriors signing Georges Niang, Brandon Williams: How they fit with Golden State
articles.summary: The Warriors are signing Brandon Williams and Georges Niang to one-year deals. Here's how the players fit with Golden State.
articles.body:
The Golden State Warriors have had a rather quiet offseason that returned many familiar faces from last season's roster. Now, they have added two newcomers at the guard and forward positions.

The Warriors agreed to sign 6-foot-1 point guard Brandon Williams to a one-year, $2.6 million deal, according to ESPN NBA insider Shams Charania . Golden State also agreed to sign free agent forward Georges Niang to a one-year, $3.9 million deal, Charania reported.

Williams spent the 2025-26 season with the Dallas Mavericks , where he averaged career highs with 13 points and 3.9 assists in 66 games. Williams averaged 22.2 minutes per night, the most playing time he's seen since joining the NBA as an undrafted rookie signing in 2021.

Williams was on the Mavericks' roster the previous three seasons. He first entered the league playing for the Portland Trail Blazers , where he averaged 12.9 points in 24 games in 2021-22.

The veteran Niang has averaged 7.4 points per game across 544 NBA games, but did not play in 2025-26 due to injury.

The fifth-year NBA player joins a guard-heavy team already featuring the likes of Stephen Curry , Brandin Podziemski , Moses Moody , Will Richard , LJ Cryer , Gary Payton II and De'Anthony Melton.

Williams will seemingly be a spark off the bench for Golden State. It's a role Williams is familiar with and the Warriors know how dynamic he can be torching other second units − they got a taste of that work last season.

Williams had one of his best games against the Warriors on Christmas Day 2025, while with the Mavericks. Williams seemingly couldn't miss that day. He tallied 26 points on 9-for-12 shooting from the field.

He scored a career-high against the Memphis Grizzlies on March 7, 2025 when he went off for 31 points on 10-for-15 shooting, including 4-of-8 on 3-point field goals. He added six assists, five rebounds and a steal to his stat line. Williams showcased his ability to get to the rim and draw contact that game, getting to the free throw line eight times, making seven.

If healthy, Niang brings another 3-point shooting threat to the Warriors roster. He fits in all too well.

After a decade in the NBA, Niang has proved to be a reliable role player and credible 3-point shooter who connects from deep at a 40% clip for his career.

Niang missed the 2025-26 season due to a foot injury. The Warriors were all too familiar with injuries last season, with Curry, Moody, Jimmy Butler III and Al Horford among the big names impacted.

Niang has played for the Indiana Pacers , Utah Jazz , Philadelphia 76ers , Cleveland Cavaliers and Atlanta Hawks . He was going to return to the Jazz after a trade last offseason because the team felt his veteran presence would benefit their young core. Niang joining the Warriors' mix of veteran leadership and young reserves should be the perfect storm.

Plus, Niang should be somewhat familiar with the Warriors' organization and development system having played for their G-League affiliate, the Santa Cruz Warriors, during the 2017-18 season.

Williams won't have too much of a time getting acclimated with the Warriors and how they operate. He is already familiar with a member of the team.

Williams is a 26-year-old guard from Los Angeles . He attended Crespi Carmelite High School in Encino, California, where he was teammates with Melton. They dominated the floor when they shared the space. Melton averaged 20 points and Williams averaged 15.8 points as they led the Celts to a 33-5 record and won the CIF Division I state championship.

The two celebrated Williams' signing, posting a screen grab from their FaceTime video call showing both smiling as Williams quoted the tagline for hip-hop producer Chandler "Turbo" Durham.

"RUN IT BACK TURBOOOO @DeAnthonyMelton," Williams posted on X, formerly Twitter, with blue and yellow hearts symbolizing the Warriors' color-scheme.

RUN IT BACK TURBOOOO @DeAnthonyMelton 💛💙 pic.twitter.com/tyoarMA0R7 — Brandon Williams (@TheeBWill) August 25, 2026

RUN IT BACK TURBOOOO @DeAnthonyMelton 💛💙 pic.twitter.com/tyoarMA0R7

Although not Southern California, Williams is back on the West Coast, so that has to be a breath of fresh air for him. His familiarity with Melton should help make for a smooth transition to the Bay Area.
paragraphs: The Golden State Warriors have had a rather quiet offseason that returned many familiar faces from last season's roster. Now, they have added two newcomers at the guard and forward positions.

The Warriors agreed to sign 6-foot-1 point guard Brandon Williams to a one-year, $2.6 million deal, according to ESPN NBA insider Shams Charania . Golden State also agreed to sign free agent forward Georges Niang to a one-year, $3.9 million deal, Charania reported.

Williams spent the 2025-26 season with the Dallas Mavericks , where he averaged career highs with 13 points and 3.9 assists in 66 games. Williams averaged 22.2 minutes per night, the most playing time he's seen since joining the NBA as an undrafted rookie signing in 2021.
Williams was on the Mavericks' roster the previous three seasons. He first entered the league playing for the Portland Trail Blazers , where he averaged 12.9 points in 24 games in 2021-22.
The veteran Niang has averaged 7.4 points per game across 544 NBA games, but did not play in 2025-26 due to injury.
The fifth-year NBA player joins a guard-heavy team already featuring the likes of Stephen Curry , Brandin Podziemski , Moses Moody , Will Richard , LJ Cryer , Gary Payton II and De'Anthony Melton.

Williams will seemingly be a spark off the bench for Golden State. It's a role Williams is familiar with and the Warriors know how dynamic he can be torching other second units − they got a taste of that work last season.

Williams had one of his best games against the Warriors on Christmas Day 2025, while with the Mavericks. Williams seemingly couldn't miss that day. He tallied 26 points on 9-for-12 shooting from the field.

He scored a career-high against the Memphis Grizzlies on March 7, 2025 when he went off for 31 points on 10-for-15 shooting, including 4-of-8 on 3-point field goals. He added six assists, five rebounds and a steal to his stat line. Williams showcased his ability to get to the rim and draw contact that game, getting to the free throw line eight times, making seven.
If healthy, Niang brings another 3-point shooting threat to the Warriors roster. He fits in all too well.
After a decade in the NBA, Niang has proved to be a reliable role player and credible 3-point shooter who connects from deep at a 40% clip for his career.
Niang missed the 2025-26 season due to a foot injury. The Warriors were all too familiar with injuries last season, with Curry, Moody, Jimmy Butler III and Al Horford among the big names impacted.

Niang has played for the Indiana Pacers , Utah Jazz , Philadelphia 76ers , Cleveland Cavaliers and Atlanta Hawks . He was going to return to the Jazz after a trade last offseason because the team felt his veteran presence would benefit their young core. Niang joining the Warriors' mix of veteran leadership and young reserves should be the perfect storm.
Plus, Niang should be somewhat familiar with the Warriors' organization and development system having played for their G-League affiliate, the Santa Cruz Warriors, during the 2017-18 season.
Williams won't have too much of a time getting acclimated with the Warriors and how they operate. He is already familiar with a member of the team.

Williams is a 26-year-old guard from Los Angeles . He attended Crespi Carmelite High School in Encino, California, where he was teammates with Melton. They dominated the floor when they shared the space. Melton averaged 20 points and Williams averaged 15.8 points as they led the Celts to a 33-5 record and won the CIF Division I state championship.
The two celebrated Williams' signing, posting a screen grab from their FaceTime video call showing both smiling as Williams quoted the tagline for hip-hop producer Chandler "Turbo" Durham.
"RUN IT BACK TURBOOOO @DeAnthonyMelton," Williams posted on X, formerly Twitter, with blue and yellow hearts symbolizing the Warriors' color-scheme.

RUN IT BACK TURBOOOO @DeAnthonyMelton 💛💙 pic.twitter.com/tyoarMA0R7

articles.title: The backlash Pride faces from inside and outside the LGBT community
articles.summary: Big companies used to go out of their way to support Pride. Now, there's a nervousness in the air, Darren Milby writes
articles.body:
Matt left Crewe as soon as he could, aged 18, feeling that he wasn't accepted as a young gay man. The only LGBT scene to mention was a tiny, makeshift bar behind a curtain in the back of an out-of-town pub.

He left in 2015, but this June found himself returning home, for Crewe Pride.

For Matt, it was a significant homecoming. "It really took me back to when I was a kid growing up here, trying to navigate my identity. It felt so important to be there and see how a town that wasn't particularly welcoming… has changed and flourished."

For many, these small, community Pride events feel a world away from the huge celebrations in the UK's largest cities.

But Matt's happy weekend in Crewe masks a growing culture war over Pride. Over the last few years, a number of councils have withdrawn their support for Pride festivals, while some big brands - perhaps nervous about being seen as too "woke" - have become hesitant to associate themselves with them. On top of all that, there's a long-running complaint from some LGBT campaigners that Pride has become overly commercialised; while the argument over trans issues has also made matters more fraught.

It's leading some to ask: what future do Pride events have?

Pride started as a protest, with Britain's first official Pride march in London in 1972. Homosexuality was illegal in the UK until 1967, and LGBT people lost jobs and housing because of their sexuality, while police forces frequently targeted the community with raids and surveillance that made everyday life precarious.

In Manchester, Pride started small in 1985. A bring‑and‑buy sale on Canal Street was organised to raise money to spruce up the rather drab-looking hospital ward treating those with HIV and Aids at the height of the epidemic.

Little did those early attendees realise how big Manchester Pride would become: a four-day, city centre extravaganza over the August bank holiday weekend, with colourful floats, loud music, and every inch of pavement filled with enthusiastic spectators dressed to the nines, streaked with rainbow face paint.

By 2019, the event had outgrown the city's famous Gay Village. That year's headline act, American superstar Ariana Grande, performed in a purpose-built stage in another part of Manchester - for a premium ticket price. It prompted criticism, and the organisers of Manchester Pride would later come under fire for ending funding for various charities (including an HIV charity, and a scheme that distributed free condoms).

The company behind Manchester Pride went into voluntary liquidation last year, owing more than £1m to suppliers and performers, including Nelly Furtado. Since its collapse, local businesses and charities have created a not-for-profit group - Manchester Village Pride - with the aim of organising a much cheaper festival more rooted in the community.

Carl Austin-Behan, who is helping to organise this year's scaled-back event, says he's been "frustrated for a number of years" by the direction of Manchester Pride. "When things were being taken out of the village, that was the first sign that things were going in the wrong direction… It should be about the community. We certainly don't need to be spending the amount of money that was spent on Manchester Pride."

And Manchester's problems aren't isolated. London Pride has faced criticism for feeling overly corporate and overcrowded; Brighton has struggled with the financial burden of staging large‑scale concerts and policing. Against that backdrop, smaller events like Crewe seem to be the direction many Prides are going in 2026.

But the political winds have also changed - with seemingly less corporate enthusiasm for diversity and inclusion initiatives.

Phil Douglas, organiser of Newcastle Pride, says: "There is a general nervousness from organisations and companies to be front and centre in their support. We see some wanting to still support us but not wanting their logo attached… they don't want the backlash which is right there ready in the online community. It's quite a complex time to navigate support for Prides as a whole."

A few years ago, you couldn't go on social media in June - known as "Pride month" - without seeing what felt like every corporate logo incorporating the Pride flag. Critics called it "rainbow‑washing", arguing that the displays of solidarity were more about marketing than meaningful action.

But now, according to Guardian analysis, the corporate presence has been waning. Last year, mentions of Pride on social media by the UK's 10 biggest listed or headquartered companies had fallen by 92% compared with 2023 - a drop that suggests brands are pulling back from overt LGBT messaging.

"There has been a general rowing back of corporate support for LGBT causes globally," says Paul Martin, chief executive of the LGBT Foundation charity. "We've seen that with politics changing in some countries and diversity and inclusion being seen as too woke… We don't get support from some quarters like we used to.

"And that has played out with Pride festivals as well. Corporate funding has been pulled back and that has caused a real challenge for Pride organisers to balance the books."

A survey by the pollster Ipsos found that the share of British adults who want companies and brands to promote LGBT rights dipped from 52% in 2021 to 44% this year.

In Liverpool, Merseyside Police did not take part in the city's Pride parade last year after legal advice warned that uniformed participation by a public body could breach rules on political impartiality.

This summer, firefighters and police again stayed away: Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service said it was taking a "pragmatic approach" following a High Court ruling that found officers in the north‑east should not have been allowed to join a Pride event. West Midlands Ambulance Service also withdrew from Birmingham Pride on similar legal advice.

Back in May's local elections in England, Reform UK won power on 14 councils, adding to the 10 they already controlled. Last month, the party's leader, Nigel Farage, said he is "fine" with Pride events going ahead but did not want local authorities to promote them.

A few weeks after taking power in Durham last year, the town's new Reform administration removed a rainbow flag from the council headquarters. Councillors also withdrew their funding contribution of £2,500 for Durham Pride. In the Merseyside town of St Helens, meanwhile, the Reform council leader instructed officials to cease engagement with all aspects of Pride; the council also removed displays celebrating the festival from libraries.

Explaining the cuts to funding, Reform's Darren Grimes, deputy leader of Durham Council, says: "I feel that we've moved away from that laudable aim of gay equality. We achieved same-sex marriage and that was the final frontier."

Durham Pride organiser Mel Metcalf says taking the flag down made LGBT people in the community "feel unwelcome". The festival did still take place; organisers said it was their "biggest" year ever, after raising around £25,000 from individual donors and trade unions.

As well as Reform's approach, the new Conservative council leader in Enfield, north London, has said they will only fly certain flags outside Enfield Civic Centre - and the rainbow flag is not one of them.

Debate around trans rights is also fuelling the Pride culture war. Some gay and lesbian people who describe themselves as "gender critical" - and whose beliefs mean they're sceptical of some of the aims of the trans rights movement - say they feel sidelined by Pride; while some trans people say they no longer feel safe attending.

A lesbian woman who describes herself as gender critical, and did not want to be named, told me she no longer attends Pride because she thinks it has become dominated by a focus on trans issues.

Grimes, one of Reform's highest-profile gay members, argues that Pride has moved away from its focus on gay equality and become bound up with the wider gender identity debate: "You've slain the dragon in the pursuit of equality and now all you are left with is a few rambling sheep." He says that "public subsidy" for LGBT issues has become a "cash cow" that fuels "narratives of victimhood".

For some, the focus on trans rights is a reason to step back from Pride; for others, it underscores why events like Sparkle matter.

Sparkle is the UK's biggest transgender celebration. It takes place in late June in Manchester's Gay Village, a few months before the Pride weekend. This year's event had live music and comedy. Lauren, a transgender volunteer at the event, told me: "We've got a lot of stigma and hatred against us… You've got people trying to push us back into the dark and it does make it harder to live our lives."

Another transgender woman I spoke to, who was staying in a hotel in Manchester's Gay Village, said she wanted to be in the city for the event, but was wary of leaving the hotel because she felt unsafe.

Security has also become a central consideration, especially after the events of last month in Berlin, when 21-year-old Abdul Ballout drove a car into a crowd at the city's Pride festival, killing one woman and injuring 29 others. Guy Mathias, from the Security Commonwealth - a trade group for security firms - says he thinks many Pride organisers will review their plans following the Berlin attack.

"Smaller events generally would cost less individually, but they still need many of the same safety measures in place," he adds.

Others think that Pride festivals can create headaches for local residents. Andy Winter, a columnist for the Brighton Argus, attended Pride marches in the 1980s in his role as a Brighton councillor. He recalled in one piece how he was vilified by the press at the time for supporting a pro-LGBT council motion. But last year, he wrote that Brighton's Pride weekend comes with "alcohol and drug-fuelled excesses".

He wrote: "Even though I am not gay, Pride impacts on me. One of the parks I use is 'closed' for ten days... to allow largely straight performers to entertain those able to pay the large entry fee." He added: "The streets are littered with plastics and broken glass. I pity neighbours of the park and surrounding streets who see their driveways and gardens used as toilets."

I've been to dozens of Pride events over the years. Manchester has always been a must. When I was a teenager in Ulverston, Cumbria - a place where I was pretty certain I was the only gay in the village - Manchester always seemed like the bright lights, a land where you could be free and your true self.

This year I'll return again, excited to catch up with my friends and intrigued to see what the new community-focused Pride is all about.

But I suspect there'll be a slightly different mood in the air this year; an awareness that in some parts of the country, Pride has become controversial.

Younger LGBT people still say Pride matters. A 2024 YouGov survey of more than 500 LGBT Britons, aged 16 to 24, found that 90% say it is "very" or "fairly" important that Pride month still exists.

As a young man, I eventually left Ulverston to live in Manchester. But this summer I took a trip back to my old hometown for their Pride festival, a tradition still in its infancy.

The once-familiar cobbled streets looked so different to how I remembered them, lined with cheering locals clapping and filming on phones as a procession bedecked in rainbow flags swept past, led by a brass band playing upbeat gay anthems. It felt a world away from Manchester's famous pop stars and stages covered in corporate logos.

Matt had a similar reflection on returning to Crewe. "What really resonated with me and blew my mind was the fact that it was so family-centred. These small towns put on events that are for the community first and foremost."

As I looked around Ulverston, the national debates that have shaped Pride in recent years felt distant. I was distracted by the small things: people laughing, the spread of ages in attendance. It was the community my teenage self never would have imagined he'd see.

articles.title: ‘I’m Not Taking Back a Single Thing’ — Paul Finebaum Refuses To Back Down From Red-Flagging Curt Cignetti’s Indiana in Bold 2026 Prediction
articles.summary: Can the Hoosiers win back-to-back national championships? College football analyst Paul Finebaum does not think so. In fact, after making a bold prediction a...
articles.body:
Can the Hoosiers win back-to-back national championships? College football analyst Paul Finebaum does not think so. In fact, after making a bold prediction about it, he received online backlash.

Now, he's come back and doubled down on his take.

Paul Finebaum Reiterates 2026 Bold Prediction for Indiana Hoosiers

Finebaum didn't mince words with his recent bold prediction regarding the Hoosiers. After a fairy-tale season a year ago, Finebaum says people need to chill out on Indiana in 2026.

The college football analyst recently said Indiana is not winning the national championship this season, and plenty of people came after him for that take.

On Tuesday, he got a chance to respond on "First Take," and he took the opportunity to double down.

"I am not taking back a single thing. Maybe I could have said it nicer. Maybe I could have been more diplomatic," Finebaum said . "I didn't know a single Indiana graduate until midway through last season, and now they are literally falling out of Amazon trucks. I don't know what's going on here."

Finebaum predicted the Hoosiers would finish the regular season 10-2 and make the playoffs, but doesn't have belief in Indiana past that point.

"I think Indiana is a really good team. I predicted they'll go to the playoffs. They're probably 10-2. I'm worried about their offensive line," Finebaum said. "Worried about the secondary. Worried about the quarterback. Yes, the schedule, which I went into.

"I can't wait to hear you brag a little bit more because your time of bragging is about over."

PREDICT THE CFB SEASON: PFN's Free CFB Playoff Predictor

Finebaum's last sentence was targeted at "First Take" host Shae Cornette, who is an Indiana graduate.

While Finebaum doesn't believe the Hoosiers will go back-to-back, he doesn't think the program's run last season was a fluke. Curt Cignetti certainly started something at Indiana, and many believe he'll keep it going for years to come.

However, the Hoosiers had a lot of moving parts this offseason, with players heading to the NFL, led by Heisman Trophy winner Fernando Mendoza.

MORE: 'One of the Worst College Football Coaches I Have Ever Seen' — Paul Finebaum Ethers Bill Belichick Amid UNC's 'Mass Chaos'

They had to be active in the transfer portal, and they were. But getting all of those new pieces to work together is easier said than done.

According to PFN's College Football Power Rankings , the program enters the program as the No. 3-ranked team in the country with a 27.50 rating, trailing only Ohio State (28.75) and Oregon (27.75).

articles.title: Wood fire prompts evacuations in Riverside County
articles.summary: A fire in an incoporated area of Perris has prompted evacuation orders and warnings, authorities said.
articles.body:
A fire in Riverside County has prompted evacuation orders and warnings in the Inland Empire.

The Wood fire was burning near Orland and Roth roads in an unincorporated portion of Perris, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection. It comes amid an extreme heat warning in many parts of Southern California, including in the valleys of San Bernardino and Riverside counties, for "dangerously hot conditions" with high temperatures up to 110 degrees.

The fire had burned about 60 acres as of 3 p.m. and is 0% contained, according to Cal Fire.

At 4:30 p.m., there were road closures on Salter Road at Fox Street, and at Juniper Road and Ida Leona Road.

Nearly 170 personnel have been deployed to respond to the fire, including three helicopters and 29 engines, Cal Fire said.

Officials issued evacuation orders for zones RVC-1060 and RVC-1059 shortly after 2 p.m., warning of "immediate threat to life." The evacuation area is bounded roughly by Orange Avenue to the north, Juniper Road to the west, Santa Rosa Mine Road and San Jacinto Avenue to the south and Old Elsinore Road to the east. An evacuation map can be found here .

Evacuees, and their pets, can go to the Perris Library at 163 E. San Jacinto Ave. for shelter and other resources, according to the order.

Officials also issued evacuation warnings for surrounding neighborhoods. The cause of the fire is under investigation, and it was not immediately known if there had been civilian injuries or structural damage.

Most of Harford Springs Reserve, a park featuring several hiking trails, is under an evacuation warning, according to the map. The northwestern part of Motte Rimrock Reserve, a biological field station on a rocky plateau managed by UC Riverside, also falls in an evacuation warning zone.

The blaze was reported just before 1 p.m. near the area of Rider Street and Dreamglo Lane, Cal Fire/Riverside County Fire Department posted on X. The fire was, at the time, burning at a "dangerous rate in medium grass and brush."

By 2:15 p.m., the agency said the fire was burning at a "moderate rate."

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .
